query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted aging heat treatment that promotes the precipitation of fine, coherent γ′‑like phases in a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature yield strength relative to the same alloy without the aging treatment.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy whose principal constituents are titanium and nickel (with three additional elements each in the 5–35 at% range to meet the HEA definition) produced as a fully homogenized single-phase (or nearly single-phase) solid solution by conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Apply an optimized post-solidification aging heat treatment under controlled temperature and time conditions that induce the nucleation and growth of nano-scale, coherent precipitates (γ′‑like phase) within the bulk alloy.
generation.conditions: The alloy is held at an elevated aging temperature (within the window that permits fine precipitation without coarsening, where the temperature is below the matrix melting point and high enough to allow atomic diffusion) for a controlled aging time. The elevated-temperature mechanical properties are measured during a tensile/compression test at the target service temperature for high-temperature applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of uniformly distributed, coherent nano-precipitates (γ′‑like phase) within the titanium–nickel rich matrix.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion at high temperatures. Their coherent interface with the matrix creates an effective precipitate strengthening mechanism, thereby raising the yield strength during high-temperature operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aged alloy will exhibit an improved elevated-temperature yield strength (and associated creep resistance) compared to the as-homogenized, unaged baseline sample. The magnitude of improvement is qualitatively expected to be significant but its precise value remains uncertain.
generation.baseline: The same titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy produced without the post‐solidification aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable only within the compositional bounds of HEAs (each element between 5–35 at%) where titanium and nickel serve as the primary constituents, and is effective so long as the aging temperature and time are maintained within the process window that avoids excessive precipitate coarsening or deleterious phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: While the precipitation strengthening mechanism is well established in related systems, the exact aging parameters (temperature and time) and the quantitative improvement in yield strength at the service temperature are uncertain and need to be experimentally optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy with identical compositions and processing histories except for the post-solidification treatment. The experimental group undergoes the proposed aging heat treatment designed to precipitate nano-scale γ′‑like phases, while the control group is retained in the homogenized, unaged state. Subsequently, both batches are subjected to identical elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or creep tests) and microstructural analysis via TEM and XRD.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength (or creep resistance) measured at the intended service temperature.
Microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD) to confirm the presence, size, and distribution of the γ′‑like precipitates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength (or if the expected fine, coherent precipitates are not observed in the microstructure) relative to the control group under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have gained considerable attention due to their innovative design and outstanding mechanical properties []. HEAs consist of 5~35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, resulting in high configurational entropy, significant lattice distortion, and reduced diffusion rates []. HEAs are typically characterized by configurational entropies exceeding 1.5R (where R is the gas constant) []. The configurational entropy equation is shown in Equation (1). where Δsmix is the constituent entropy, N is the number of elements, and xi is the entropy of each element. Due to their high entropy, HEAs tend to form single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. This unique composition and microstructure give HEAs exceptional mechanical properties. HEAs generally exhibit a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structure []. Unlike typical alloys, HEAs form a concentrated solid solution. Consequently, HEAs exhibit high strength and hardness at room temperature, along with excellent mechanical performance at both low and high temperatures [].

One of the most intensely investigated HEA systems, primarily forming cubic phases is AlCoCrCuFeNi [,]. Due to the positive enthalpy of mixing ∆Hmix among Cu and the elements Fe and Cr, segregation was observed, deteriorating mechanical and corrosion properties. Therefore, subsequent investigations focused on the copper-free derivative AlCoCrFeNi [,,,,]. Early studies concentrated on the equimolar composition. However, investigations showed that optimum properties are usually achieved when choosing a differing chemical composition []. Investigating the influence of different alloying elements showed a strong influence of aluminium on the microstructure, phase composition, and properties [,]. For a low aluminium content, fcc phases are stabilised, whereas high contents of aluminium act as a strong bcc phase stabiliser [,]. In addition, the formation of complex phases can be suppressed for a high aluminium content []. Furthermore, the influence of additional alloying elements has been investigated.
